190.title: Sudama's handful of rice
190.hook: a poor man brings the richest friend in the world a handful of flattened rice
190.carry: bhakti: a leaf given with love is enough
190.howItsDone: In daily puja many Hindus offer flowers, tulsi or bilva leaves, fruit and water at the home shrine; Gita 9.26 is often recited to explain that what matters is the love, not the size of the offering.

segments.voice: Yesterday, raja-guhya, the royal secret: all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky. Your line was all beings rest in God, like wind in the sky. Today, what someone can bring to the one who holds everything.
screen: `RAJA-GUHYA — ALL BEINGS REST IN GOD, LIKE WIND IN THE SKY.`

segments.voice: A poor Brahmin, the one later tellings call Sudama, has barely enough to feed his family. As a boy he studied with Krishna. Now Krishna is a king in a golden city, and Sudama's wife begs him to visit his old friend. But what do you bring a king? He borrows a few handfuls of flattened rice and ties them in a corner of his worn cloth. At the palace, Krishna runs to hug him, washes his feet, and then notices the little bundle he's trying to hide. What's that you've brought me?
screen: `A POOR MAN. A KING FOR A FRIEND.` → `A HANDFUL OF FLATTENED RICE.` → `WHAT'S THAT YOU'VE BROUGHT ME?`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's telling, Krishna takes the rice and eats it with delight, and he speaks words that are also a verse of the Gita, the one that crowns today's reading: whoever offers me with love a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, I accept that offering of love from the one whose heart is pure. Gita nine, twenty-six. Patram, pushpam, phalam, toyam. Nothing costly; anyone can find them. The verses before it build the scene. Krishna says fools look past him in human form, but great souls, verse fourteen says, are always singing about him, bowing, steady in their vows. He is the ritual and the offering, the fire and the ghee, verse sixteen. He is the father of the world, verse seventeen; the mother, the grandparent; the goal, the support, the lord, the witness, the home, the refuge, the friend. Verse twenty-two: to those who worship me alone, always united with me, I bring what they lack and protect what they have. So when the Lord of everything gets to name what he wants, he names a leaf. Not because the gift is big, but because the love is real. The word the verse leans on is bhakti: devotion, love turned toward God. And Sudama, the story says, walked home without having asked for anything, and found his hut had become a palace.

segments.voice: Hold something small in your open hands, a glass of water, a leaf, a flower, a piece of fruit, or simply picture one, and think of what you'd offer with it: thanks, a worry, a person you love. If you pray, you can offer it to God, as the verse says; if not, simply hold it with care, as if it were a gift.
Bhakti. Devotion, love turned toward God. Gita nine, twenty-six: a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water, offered with love, is accepted.

191.title: Whatever you do, offer it
191.hook: the women of Mathura envy the milkmaids who sang of Krishna while they churned; one verse turns the whole day into an offering
191.carry: arpana: every ordinary act can be offered
191.tomorrow: The robber who became a poet
191.howItsDone: Many Hindus try to dedicate their daily work as an offering in the spirit of Gita 9.27; some sing or repeat God's name while they work, and some close a meal or a task with 'Krishnarpanam', offered to Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakti: Sudama's handful of rice, and the one who offers a leaf. Your line was a leaf given with love is enough. Today the offering gets much bigger.

Krishna has grown up and left the cowherd village. In Mathura, the tyrant Kamsa sets him to wrestle the king's champions in a packed arena. The women of the city watch from the stands, and the Bhagavata Purana gives them a line nobody expects. They don't envy the queens or the sages. They envy the milkmaids back in Vraja. Lucky are they, the women say: while they milk the cows, pound the grain, churn the butter, sweep the floors and rock their crying babies, they sing about him. Their chores were already worship.
screen: `A WRESTLING ARENA IN MATHURA.` → `THEY ENVY THE MILKMAIDS.` → `THEY SING OF HIM WHILE THEY CHURN.`

segments.voice: Years later, on the battlefield, Krishna puts the same idea into one verse. Verse twenty-seven: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, whatever discipline you practice, Arjuna, do it as an offering to me. In Sanskrit it's a list with a drumbeat: yat karoshi, whatever you do; yad ashnasi, whatever you eat; yaj juhoshi, whatever you offer into the fire; dadasi yat, whatever you give; yat tapasyasi, whatever effort you make. Five whatevers, and one instruction: tat kurushva mad-arpanam, make it an offering to me. Look at the list. Eating comes second, right next to sacrifice. Yesterday Krishna asked for a leaf. Today he asks for the whole day: not more stuff, more of your ordinary life, turned toward him. That's the women of Vraja. They didn't stop churning to pray; the churning became the prayer. Verse twenty-eight says what happens: you'll be freed from the bonds of action, with its good and bad fruits, and you'll come to me. Some readers hear chapter three's work without attachment here: it's hard to clutch the fruit of something you've already given away. This is arpana, offering, and it's why some families close a meal or a task with a quiet word: Krishnarpanam, offered to Krishna.

segments.voice: Pick one chore you'll do today: the dishes, the laundry, the walk to the bus. Do it the way the women of Vraja did, with a name, a song or a thought of God running underneath it. If you pray, you can say at the end, as some families do, offered to Krishna. If not, simply do it with care, as if handing it to someone you love.
Arpana. Offering, handing over. Gita nine, twenty-seven: whatever you do, eat, offer, give or strive for, make it an offering.
Your line: arpana, every ordinary act can be offered. The dishes too. Day one hundred ninety-one, offered.

192.title: The robber who became a poet
192.hook: a highway robber becomes a poet; the Gita says the door was never locked
192.carry: bhakti is open to anyone who turns
192.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold that devotion to God is open to everyone regardless of birth or past, and the story of Valmiki, the robber who became the poet of the Ramayana, is widely told to show that anyone can turn.

segments.voice: Yesterday, arpana: whatever you do, eat, give or strive for, make it an offering. Your line was every ordinary act can be offered. Today, the end of chapter nine.

Valmiki, the poet of the Ramayana, was once a highway robber, or so the story people tell goes, stopping travelers in the forest. One day he stopped a sage, who asked him a simple question: your family shares what you steal, but will they share the wrongs you did to get it? The robber went home and asked. They said no. He came back shaken, and the sage gave him the name of Rama to repeat. He sat repeating it so long that an anthill grew over him. And he came out a poet.
screen: `A ROBBER IN THE FOREST.` → `WILL YOUR FAMILY SHARE THE WRONG?` → `HE CAME OUT A POET.`

segments.voice: Verse twenty-nine: I am the same to all beings. No one is hateful to me, and no one is my favorite. But those who worship me with love are in me, and I am in them. Then verse thirty, the one that surprises people: even if someone of very bad conduct worships me with undivided devotion, they should be considered good, because they've made the right resolve. Not good eventually. Good now, because of which way they've turned. Verse thirty-one: quickly they become righteous and reach lasting peace. And Krishna tells Arjuna to announce it: my devotee never perishes. Na me bhaktah pranashyati. Verse thirty-two widens the circle. Those who take refuge in me, even those the society of the time held low, women, merchants and farmers, laborers, reach the highest goal. The verse names groups the ranking of its day placed below others, and readers today argue about its wording; some find it painful, some read it as those groups being singled out for welcome. Some hear a widening: doors that were closed, pushed open. Verse thirty-four, the chapter's last, is the whole of it in a line: fix your mind on me, be devoted to me, offer to me, bow to me, and you'll come to me. In the Gita's telling, nobody is too far gone to turn.
screen: `THE SAME TO ALL BEINGS.` · `EVEN THE WORST, TURNED, IS GOOD.` · `MY DEVOTEE NEVER PERISHES.` · `A WIDER CIRCLE, READ TWO WAYS.` · then, large: `NO ONE IS OUTSIDE.`

segments.voice: Think of someone you've written off: someone who hurt you, a public figure, maybe a younger version of yourself. You don't have to excuse anything they did; just hold them for a moment in the light of verse thirty, that turning is always possible. Breathe in and picture the door open; breathe out and let a little of the hardness go.
Bhakta. Devotee, one who loves God. Gita nine, thirty: whoever turns with undivided devotion, whatever they've done, is to be counted good. No one is outside.
Your line: bhakti is open to anyone who turns. The door stays open, whatever's behind you. Chapter nine, complete.

193.title: Brahma and the endless stalk
193.hook: the creator god climbs down his lotus stalk looking for where he came from, and never finds the bottom
193.carry: the source of all has no source
193.tomorrow: In which forms should I think of you?
193.howItsDone: Many Hindus hold that one reality, Brahman, is the source of every god and being; many gather for satsang to sing and talk about God, which Gita 10.9 describes as devotees awakening one another, and 10.8 is often recited for its picture of God as the source of all.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhakta: Valmiki the robber, and even the worst, turned toward God, counted good. Your line was bhakti is open to anyone who turns. Today, chapter ten opens.

At the dawn of a new creation, the Bhagavata Purana says, the old world had dissolved into endless waters, and Vishnu lay resting on them. From his navel a lotus rose, and on the lotus sat Brahma, the creator god, his four faces looking four ways. And he saw nothing at all. Who am I? he wondered. Where did this lotus come from? So he climbed down into the hollow stalk, down and down, for ages, looking for its root. He never found the bottom. At last he climbed back up, sat still, steadied his breath and turned inward. And there, in his own heart, he saw the one he'd been looking for.
screen: `A LOTUS FROM VISHNU'S NAVEL.` → `BRAHMA CLIMBS DOWN THE STALK.` → `NO BOTTOM. THEN, THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Chapter ten of the Gita opens with the same lesson. Krishna says he'll speak again, because Arjuna delights in hearing. Verse two: neither the gods nor the great sages know my origin, because I am the origin of the gods and the sages, in every way. That's Brahma in the stalk. Even the creator can't climb down to the source, because he is downstream of it. This is one of Hinduism's biggest ideas: one ultimate reality, which the Upanishads call Brahman, behind every god, every being and every thing. In the Gita, Krishna speaks as that source. Verse eight: I am the source of all; from me everything moves. Then a list that's easy to rush past. Understanding, patience, truth, calm. Pleasure and pain. Birth and death. Fear and fearlessness. All these, verse five says, come from me alone. Even the hard things share one spring. Verse nine pictures what the wise do: they talk about him together and wake each other up, bodhayantah parasparam. That's the spirit of satsang, the gathering many Hindus keep to sing and speak of God. And verse eleven ends where Brahma ended: living in their hearts, out of compassion, I destroy the darkness with the shining lamp of knowledge. You won't find the source by climbing down. It's found within.
screen: `EVEN THE GODS DON'T KNOW MY ORIGIN.` · `I AM THE SOURCE OF ALL.` · `EVEN PAIN AND FEAR, ONE SPRING.` · `THE LAMP IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE SOURCE HAS NO SOURCE.`

segments.voice: Sit still, the way Brahma did when he stopped searching. Follow your breath back as far as you can: the air in the room, the trees and oceans behind it. Then stop following, and rest your attention at the center of your chest, where verse eleven says the lamp is lit. If you pray, you can hold verse eight in mind: from you, everything moves. If not, simply rest in the quiet.
The source. Gita ten, eight: Krishna says he is the origin of all, and from him everything moves. Even Brahma came from it.
Your line: the source of all has no source. Brahma searched the stalk; the answer was in his heart. See you tomorrow.

194.title: In which forms should I think of you?
194.hook: Arjuna believes Krishna is everything, then asks where to look; why Hindus pray before a murti
194.howItsDone: Most Hindu homes keep a murti or picture of God at a shrine; many Hindus explain it as Arjuna's question suggests: God is everywhere, and the image is where you place your eyes and your love.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the source: even Brahma couldn't find the root of his lotus. Your line was the source of all has no source. Today, Arjuna has a question.

Picture the chariot, parked between two armies. For nine chapters, Krishna, Arjuna's friend and driver, has been telling him what's real: the self in every heart, the one all beings rest in, and yesterday, the source of everything, even the gods. Arjuna believes it. He says so, out loud. And then this warrior, the finest archer of his age, admits he doesn't know where to aim. You're everything, he says, and I believe it. But how do I think of you? In which things, which forms?
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN TWO ARMIES.` → `YOU'RE EVERYTHING. I BELIEVE IT.` → `BUT WHERE DO I LOOK?`

segments.voice: Verse twelve is Arjuna's confession of faith. You are the highest Brahman, the highest home, the eternal divine person, the first god, unborn, all-pervading. The sages say so, he adds: Narada, Asita and Devala, Vyasa. And now you say it yourself. Verse fourteen: I accept everything you've told me as true. Verse fifteen: only you know yourself, by yourself, god of gods, lord of the world. Then verse sixteen: tell me your divine glories, vibhutis, the powers by which you fill all these worlds. And verse seventeen: how shall I know you, master of yoga? In which things, in which forms, should I think of you? Verse eighteen: tell me again, in detail; your words are nectar, and I never tire of them. It's a humble question, and a deeply Hindu one. Hindus hold that God is infinite and everywhere. And yet in most Hindu homes there's a shrine with a murti, an image of Krishna, Ganesha or the Goddess, a lamp and a flower in front of it. That isn't a contradiction. Many Hindus believe God, lovingly invited, is truly present in the murti, but never only there. A person needs somewhere to put their eyes and their love, and many teachers read Arjuna's question in just this way: the infinite, met through a form. Tomorrow, Krishna's answer. Today, the question.

segments.voice: If there's a murti, a picture of God or a sacred image near you, sit facing it; if not, choose one simple thing in front of you, a candle, a plant, a patch of sky. Look at it slowly and let it be your handle, the way Arjuna asked for one. If you pray, greet God in it with folded hands, as many Hindus do each morning. If not, let it stand for something bigger than you.
Arjuna asks. After believing it all, he asks: in which forms should I think of you? Give me something to hold.
Your line: the infinite, met through forms. That's what the murti on the shelf is for. That's day one hundred ninety-four.

195.title: The taste in water
195.hook: Krishna answers Arjuna with a list: the best of every kind of thing, and one entry nobody expects
195.carry: every glory is a spark of God
195.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor the presences named in Gita chapter ten: they bathe in the Ganga, circle the sacred fig tree, chant Om and repeat a divine name (japa), seeing each as a glimpse of the divine.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Arjuna asks: in which forms should I think of you? Your line was the infinite, met through forms. Today, Krishna answers.

Pour a glass of cold water on a hot day and take a long drink. That exact clean taste when you're thirsty. Back in chapter seven, Krishna said: I am the taste in water. Not the water. The taste, the part you can't hold in your hand, that makes water water. Now Arjuna has asked where to look for him, and Krishna answers with a whole list built the same way: the best, the brightest, the deepest of every kind of thing. And somewhere in the middle, one entry that makes people stop and read it twice.
screen: `A LONG DRINK ON A HOT DAY.` → `NOT THE WATER. THE TASTE.` → `A LIST OF THE BEST OF EVERYTHING.`

segments.voice: He begins at the center. Verse twenty: I am the self seated in the heart of all beings, their beginning, their middle and their end. Then the list. Among lights, I am the radiant sun. Among bodies of water, the ocean. Among words, the single syllable Om. Among offerings, the quiet repetition of a sacred name. Among things that stand still, the Himalaya. Among trees, the sacred fig. Among rivers, the Ganga. Among letters, the letter A, the first sound. Among seasons, spring, full of flowers. And, verse thirty-three, I am time that never runs out. Now the surprise. Verse thirty-six: I am the gambling of cheats. Commentators read it more than one way. One reading: Krishna is naming whatever is the most intense of its kind, even the kind no one would choose; whatever grips hardest has a spark of his power in it. Then a wink, verse thirty-seven: among the Pandavas, I am Arjuna, the man he's talking to. Verse forty-one gives the rule for the whole list: whatever is glorious, beautiful, or mighty, know that it springs from a spark of my splendor. And the last verse: but what do you need all this detail for, Arjuna? I hold up this entire universe with a single fragment of myself. This is vibhuti, God's glory showing through the world, and it's why Hindus bathe in the Ganga, circle the sacred fig and begin with Om: each is a spark of the one splendor.
screen: `THE SELF IN THE HEART OF ALL.` · `THE SUN, THE OCEAN, OM, THE GANGA.` · `EVEN THE GAMBLING OF CHEATS.` · `A SPARK OF MY SPLENDOR.` · then, large: `EVERY GLORY, A SPARK OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Take one slow sip of water, or remember the last time you drank when you were really thirsty, and stay with the taste: the cool, the clean, the relief. Then let your attention move to the light, a sound, the air on your skin, and notice what's best in each. If you pray, you can hold verse forty-one in mind: every glory is a spark.
Rasa. Taste, flavor, essence, the part you can't hold in your hand that makes water water. Krishna's handles for the sacred: the best of each kind, every glory a spark of his splendor.
Your line: every glory is a spark of God. A sip of water, the Ganga, the letter A. On to chapter eleven tomorrow.

196.title: The divine eye
196.hook: after a week of hearing, Arjuna asks to see God's real form and is told his eyes won't do; why Hindus go for darshan
196.carry: darshan: the sight of God is a gift
196.howItsDone: Many Hindus speak of darshan, seeing and being seen by the divine, when they visit a temple; chapter eleven, where Arjuna asks to see and is given a divine eye, is often read as the Gita's great darshan.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rasa: I am the taste in water, and every glory a spark. Your line was every glory is a spark of God. Today, the end of the week, and chapter eleven begins.

Ten chapters on a chariot, and Arjuna has heard it all. This week alone: Sudama's rice; chores offered like the milkmaids' churning; the robber who became a poet; the lotus with no bottom; where to look; the taste in water. He believes every word. But hearing about someone you love isn't the same as seeing them. So the warrior turns to his friend and asks for the one thing words can't give.
screen: `TEN CHAPTERS OF HEARING.` → `HEARING ISN'T SEEING.` → `SHOW ME.`

segments.voice: Verse one: out of kindness to me you've told me this highest secret about the self, and my confusion is gone. Verse two: I've heard in detail how beings come and go, and about your greatness that doesn't end. Verse three: it is just as you say. But I want to see it: your form as the Lord of all. Then verse four, a lovely bit of humility: if you think I'm able to see it, master of yoga, show me your imperishable self. If you think I'm able. He doesn't demand. He asks, and leaves room for no. Krishna says yes. Verse five: behold my forms, by hundreds and thousands, divine, of many colors and shapes. Verse six: see the gods of the sky and the storm, wonders no one has seen before. Verse seven: see the whole universe, moving and unmoving, gathered here in my body, and anything else you want to see. Then the catch, verse eight: you can't see me with these eyes of yours, so I give you a divine eye. Divyam chakshuh. Behold my power. That's the key to the whole chapter. Seeing God isn't a matter of looking harder with ordinary eyes; the sight itself has to be given. In the Mahabharata, the narrator Sanjaya, telling all this to the blind king, has been given a divine eye too, so he can see the battlefield from the palace. That's how anyone hearing the story gets to watch. Many Hindus hear the same idea in darshan at the temple: seeing God and being seen, a sight received, not taken.
screen: `MY CONFUSION IS GONE.` · `IF YOU THINK I'M ABLE, SHOW ME.` · `NOT WITH THESE EYES.` · `A DIVINE EYE, GIVEN.` · then, large: `DARSHAN: THE SIGHT IS GIVEN.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and notice that everything you usually look at is gone, yet something is still seeing: shapes, colors, the dark behind the lids. Rest in that. Then think of one thing, or one person, you'd like to see more truly, and without forcing anything, ask in your own way, as Arjuna did: if I'm able, show me.
Divyam chakshuh. A divine eye. After hearing, Arjuna asks for sight, and Krishna gives him this eye, because ordinary eyes can't see it.
Your line: darshan, the sight of God is a gift. Arjuna asked, and left room for no. A whole week, done.
